senses.gloss:
aṅga
(‘part,’ ‘limb’)
------------------------------------------
The word which literally means part or a limb, is often used in a technical sense. For instance, in medical sciences it stands for the body or its limb. In जैनिस्म्, it stands for a class of scriptures which are twelve in number.
In वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् the word अङ्ग indicates a subordinate rite. For instance, पशुबन्ध is an अङ्ग of सोमयाग; or प्रयाज is an अङ्ग of Darśa. These subsidiary rites may or may not produce any separate result.
More often the word is used in combination with other words getting a technical flavour. Here are some samples: पञ्चाङ्ग, the five parts of an almanac like नक्षत्र or star; राज्याङ्गस्, the seven components of an imperial set-up like the king; senāṅgas, the four parts of an armed force like infantry; वेदाङ्गस्, the six subsidiary branches of knowledge which help the study of the वेदस्, like शिक्षा or the science of articulation; yajñāṅgas, the vessels used in a sacrifices like sruk and sruva (spoon and ladle) and yogāṅgas, the eight steps of योग like यम or restraint and so on.
Aṅga has often been mentioned as a country, now identified with eastern Bihar or the region around Bhagalpur in Bihar. शिव is said to have burnt मन्मथ (Cupid) to ashes here. Since मन्मथ was ultimately revived, getting back his aṅgas or limbs, the place came to be known as अङ्ग or Aṅgadeśa. This was once ruled by the well-known king Roma-pāda. During his regime there was once a severe famine. When the sage ऋष्यशृङ्ग was tactfully brought into the kingdom, it rained heavily and the people were saved from starvation.
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (2.2) mentions that अङ्ग is famous for well-bred elephants.
In the mythological lore, several kings by name अङ्ग are mentioned: a king who had joined दुर्योधन in the कुरुक्षेत्र war; a क्षत्त्रिय hero who fought the great king मान्धातृ; a क्षत्त्रिय king, the eldest son of बलि and Sudeṣṇā.
Karṇa, of the महाभारत fame, was the king of Aṅgadeśa.

Aṅgiras
------------------------------------------
One of the sages we come across, not infrequently, in the Hindu religious literature, is अङ्गिरस्. A number of Vedic hymns are attributed to him. Associated with the fire cult, he is regarded as the first sacrificer and initiator of sacred ritual. In fact, he is said to have discharged the duties of अग्नि (the fire-god) once when the latter had absconded, and thus saved the world. The mythological works describe him sometimes as a mānasaputra (mind-born son) of ब्रह्मा, the Creator and sometimes as having sprung from the sacrificial fire of god वरुण. Vasudhā, श्रद्धा, स्वधा and सती were his wives. बृहस्पति was one of his sons. The pitṛ-देवतास् (manes) are also described as his offsprings. The well-known lunar deities राका, सिनीवाली and कुहू (which are actually phases of the मोओन्) are consi-dered as his daughters.
Extolled for his great virtues, अङ्गिरस् was also a teacher of ब्रह्मविद्या, know-ledge of ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute). This explains his constant association with light, fire and luminous objects, including his identification with the planet जुपितेर् and a star in the constellation Ursa Major.
He is listed among the सप्तर्षिस् (the seven sages) of the first मन्वन्तर (the period or age of मनु). He is one of the originators of the गोत्र system. The Āṅgirases, descendants of अङ्गिरस् are stated to be kṣattriyas by birth and ब्राह्मणस् by profession. They were highly skilled in sacerdotal law, magic and traditional rites.
He is credited with the authorship of a treatise on law (Āṅgirasa Smṛti) as also on अस्त्रोनोम्य्.

aṅga and liṅga
(‘that which goes towards ब्रह्मन्’ and ‘that into which everything is dissolved’)
------------------------------------------
In वीरशैविस्म् (one of the important schools of शैविस्म्) ब्रह्मन् is called ‘Sthala’. ‘Stha’ stands for ‘sthāna’ (place) and ‘la’ for ‘laya’ (dissolution). So ‘Sthala’ is that place or source from which the universe evolves and into which it dissolves ultimately. This ‘Sthala’ divides itself out of līlā or play into लिङ्ग and अङ्ग, also called लिङ्गस्थल and अङ्गस्थल. अङ्ग is the individual सोउल् or जीव (so called because he goes back [ga] to ब्रह्मन् [aṁ] ) and लिङ्ग (= that into which everything gets dissolved, līyate) is God, शिव. अङ्ग becomes one with लिङ्ग in course of time as a result of भक्ति, upāsanā or worship. See ṢAṬSTHALA-SIDDHĀNTA for details.

aṅgamejayatva
(‘shaking of limbs’)
------------------------------------------
Patañjali, the great master of the योग system, recognizes that the principle ‘prevention is better than cure’ can be and should be applied in the path of योग also. To facilitate its practice, he has listed nine ‘antarāyas’ or obstacles to योग (Yoga-sūtras 1.30) and has added another five in a supplementary list (ibid. 1.31). He calls these as ‘vikṣepasahabhuvaḥ’ (co-existing with mental distractions). अङ्गमेजयत्व is the third obstacle in this list.
‘Aṅga’ means limb and ‘ejana’ means shaking. So अङ्गमेजयत्व is shaking or restless movement of limbs. When sorrow, disappointment and despair are not sublimated by discrimination and will-power, they cause tremendous restlessness in the मिन्द्. This affects the nervous system, getting reflected in physical restlessness. The aspirant is thus unable to sit steadily on the seat and frequently changes his position. Persisting in the practice of योग, repetition of प्रणव (Oṁ) and an attitude of surrender to God will gradually lessen this disturbance.

Aṅgad, Guru
(A. D. 1504—1552)
------------------------------------------
Sikhism, the youngest of world reli-gions, was started by गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469—1539). It was nurtured, developed and stabilized by a succession of Gurus up to गुरु Gobind Singh (A. D. 1666—1708) who declared that the sacred book, the Granth, respectfully called Guru Granth Sāhib would take the place of the गुरु thereafter.
Guru Aṅgad was the immediate successor of गुरु Nānak, chosen and anointed by Nānak himself. Before ordination his name was Lehna. Lehna who was the son of a trader called Pheru and lived in Khadur in the Punjab was a devotee of मोथेर् दुर्गा. He used to lead pilgrims to the दुर्गा तेम्प्ले and the Jvālāmukhi (a volcanic vent nearby). By chance, he once heard the recital of the famous Sikh prayer Japji and diligently sought after its author. When he finally met the गुरु Nānak his joy knew no bounds.
Then began his long tenure of single-minded and devoted service to his गुरु. During the period of internship and training he endured all the tests, trials and tribulations and earned गुरु Nānak’s confidence and faith in the fullest measure. Much against the opposition of his own wife and two sons, गुरु Nānak chose Lehna—now called Aṅgad—as his successor and anointed him as the next गुरु in A. D. 1539.
Aṅgad, though eminently fitted for the गुरु’s place, had to contend with the powerful rivalry of Siri Chand, गुरु Nānak’s eldest son, who had started the Udāsī sect, a sect with Sikh principles and an ascetic character. In course of time this sect got merged in the general body of the Sikhs, mainly due to गुरु Aṅgad’s efforts.
Another challenge he had to face was from the orthodox हिन्दुइस्म्. To keep up a distinct character for the Sikhs and सिखिस्म्, he improved upon the Gurumukhi script and committed the hymns of गुरु Nānak to writing, in that script, making it available to the common folk who got a scripture of their own, in their own language.
Aṅgad further strengthened the two institutions of laṅgar (free kitchen) and saṅgat (regular religious meetings in groups) established earlier by Nānak.
Vigorous preaching of Nānak’s doctrines, simple life in conformity with those doctrines, building a new town called Goindwal and introduction of physical culture as part of life and religion were his other contributions.
Guru Aṅgad breathed his last in 1552 at the age of forty-eight.

Aṅgada
------------------------------------------
A well-known hero of Rāmāyaṇa, अङ्गद was the son of Vālī and तारा. His exploits are many and varied. When सुग्रीव was anointed as the king of किष्किन्धा, अङ्गद was appointed as the yuvarāja, the heir apparent. He was the leader of the group of monkeys that was sent to the south in search of सीता. Before the commencement of the war, Śrī राम had sent him to रावण on a peace mission. Later, when the war was in progress he succeeded in disturbing the sacrifice at Nikumbhilā performed by इन्द्रजित्. He killed many rākṣasa heroes of रावण’s army during the battles.
There are two more Aṅgadas mentioned in the itihāsas: अङ्गद, the first son of लक्ष्मण and ऊर्मिला; अङ्गद, a क्षत्त्रिय king, who fought for दुर्योधन in the कुरुक्षेत्र war.

Āṅgirasa Smṛti
------------------------------------------
Smṛtis are law-books which prescribe the code of conduct for the individual and the society. Out of the several smṛtis known to us, Āṅgirasa Smṛti is one of the shorter works, but quoted even by authorities like याज्ञवल्क्य.
A perusal of the printed texts as also the several manuscripts available now, shows that the verses vary from 32 to 151! The book deals mainly with प्रायश्चित्त or expiation for various forbidden acts like accepting ड़ोओद् and drink from antyajas (people of lowest castes), for injuring cows as also for deadly sins. Its views on सती or sahagamana (wife dying on the funeral pyre of her dead husband) have been criticised by other works.

aṅganyāsa
(‘placing on the limbs’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu ritualistic worship has evolved into a well-developed science. Before starting the worship of the deity, all articles used in the process are to be purified, not only physically but also ceremonially. न्यास is such an act in this process, and means the ‘placing’ of gods or holy words or letters on certain parts of the body. अङ्गन्यास is an aspect of this न्यास. Also called ‘Ṣaḍaṅganyāsa’ (ṣaṭ = six, अङ्ग = limb), it involves the ceremonial purification and protection of हृदय (heart), śiras (head), śikhā (tuft), kavaca (armour, indicated by touching the shoulders with the hands crossed), netratraya (three eyes, including the middle of the eyebrows) and karatala (palm of the hand). The process is sometimes extended to more parts of the body like the feet, navel and so on.
See also KARANYĀSA and NYĀSA.

aṅgavidyā
(‘science of the limbs’)
------------------------------------------
From the ancient times, the throbbing of the limbs, particularly of the arm and the eye, has been regarded as the harbinger of coming events, auspicious or otherwise. For men, throbbing of the right side of the body is considered an auspicious sign. For women, the opposite holds good.
Some examples of such prognosti-cations can be given: The fruit indicated by the throbbing of the top of the head is the acquisition of land; of the forehead, the prosperity of the position already occupied; of the region of the eye, death; of the upper arm, union with friends; of the hand, acquisition of wealth; of the back, defeat and so on.
The Matsyapurāṇa (ch. 241) advises the placating of ब्राह्मणस् with gifts of gold to ward off the evil effects of such throbbing.
It is interesting to note that the well-known astrological work Bṛhatsaṁhitā of वराहमिहिर (6th cent. A. D.) treats of this subject (in chapter 51) in an entirely different way. When an enquirer wishes to know from the astrologer any information (for instance, about the thief who has stolen his articles), the astrologer has to closely observe the way the enquirer puts the questions touching any of his aṅgas or limbs in the process in a natural way, and prognosticate the results. For instance, if the enquirer touches his own feet in the process, the astrologer can conclude that the servant is the thief. Of course, time and place of questioning also count.

aṅgula
------------------------------------------
Out of the several units of length used in the ancient Hindu scriptures, अङ्गुल (corresponding to inch) is probably the smallest. It is variously defined as the total length of eight barley grains kept lengthwise side by side; the width of a finger; one-twelfth part of a ‘vitasti’ or span.
In इचोनोग्रफ्य्, images are recommended to be prepared according to the ‘tālamāna’ system. A ‘tāla’ is the measurement of the palm of hand (from the tip of the middle finger to the wrist) and is equal to the length of the face. Each ताल is divided into twelve ‘aṅgulas.’
